The 2026 United States Senate election in Texas will be held on November 3, 2026, to elect a member of the United States Senate to represent the state of Texas. Republican state attorney general Ken Paxton and Democratic state representative James Talarico are the nominees for their respective parties.

Four-term Republican incumbent John Cornyn sought re-election, but was challenged for the party's nomination by Paxton. After no candidate received a majority in the March 3 primary, Paxton, aided by a late endorsement from President Donald Trump, defeated Cornyn with 63.8% of the vote in a runoff on May 26. Cornyn became the first incumbent senator from Texas to lose renomination since Democrat Ralph Yarborough in 1970. In the Democratic primary, Talarico won the nomination with 52.4% of the vote over congresswoman Jasmine Crockett.

Democrats have not won a Senate election in Texas since 1988.

Background

[edit]

Texas has been considered a Republican-leaning state throughout the 21st century.[1] Democrats have not won a U.S. Senate election in the state since Lloyd Bentsen was re-elected in 1988, and they have not won any statewide election in the state since lieutenant governor Bob Bullock was re-elected in 1994.[2] Republicans have fully controlled the Texas Legislature since the 2002 elections. Texas's Republican lean has waned in the past decade, with Democrats only narrowly losing the 2018 elections for U.S. Senate and attorney general, buoyed by gains in the state's suburban areas. More recently, however, Republicans have made substantial gains with the state's Hispanic population, particularly in the Rio Grande Valley. Republican Donald Trump won the state by nearly 14 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election, while U.S. Senator Ted Cruz won re-election by over 8 points on the same ballot.[citation needed]

Incumbent Republican senator John Cornyn was first elected in 2002 to succeed fellow Republican Phil Gramm.[3] Cornyn had previously served as the state's attorney general, as well as a member of the state's Supreme Court.[4] He most recently won re-election in 2020 with 53.5% of the vote against Democrat M. J. Hegar.[5] Cornyn has a consistently conservative voting record in the U.S. Senate, and he is considered part of the Republican establishment due to his long tenure in politics.[6]

Republican primary

[edit]

Background

[edit]

Incumbent senator John Cornyn, who was seeking a fifth term, faced a competitive primary from attorney general Ken Paxton which progressed to a runoff after no candidate reached a majority in the first round. The two had clashed publicly since 2022, with Paxton criticizing Cornyn for being insufficiently conservative, particularly over his support for U.S. aid to Ukraine, DREAM Act for DACA beneficiaries and playing a leading role in the passage of the bipartisan gun safety bill after the Uvalde school massacre. Cornyn, in turn, has highlighted Paxton's legal troubles, perceived character flaws and corruption, and his 2023 impeachment, in which Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House before the Senate later acquitted him of all charges.[7][8][9][10]

The race has been seen as a key contest between the Texas Republican Party's establishment wing and its hardline conservative faction.[7] In recent years, insurgent hard-right candidates have steadily gained ground, often ousting more traditional GOP officials. Polling reflects this divide: Paxton holds a commanding lead among "Trump Movement" voters, while Cornyn performs better with the smaller group of "Traditional Republicans."[11] On May 19, 2026, Donald Trump announced his endorsement for Paxton,[12] while previously describing both Paxton and Cornyn as good friends.[13] His influence was widely seen as a key factor in determining the primary winner.[14] He had previously criticized Cornyn as a "hopeless" RINO (Republican in name only) for supporting the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, an attack Paxton's campaign highlighted in their ads.[15][16] Ted Cruz, the junior senator, avoided taking a side in the primary, though he previously endorsed Cornyn in 2020.[17]

The election takes place amid efforts by the state Republican Party to restrict its primary to registered members. Legislation to allow closed primaries failed, prompting the party to sue the state, claiming the current law violates the First Amendment.[18] Despite serving as the state's attorney general, Paxton declined to defend the law in court, drawing criticism from those who argued he would gain electorally from a closed primary.[19]

First round

[edit]

Campaign

[edit]

Paxton led Cornyn in early polling both before and after entering the race, though concerns about his general election viability persisted, as polls showed him underperforming Cornyn and, in some cases, trailing hypothetical Democratic opponents.[31] This led many Republicans to back Cornyn, as Senate GOP leaders pressed Trump for an endorsement.[32] Cornyn told The Wall Street Journal in June 2025 that he would consider stepping aside if a stronger candidate emerged to defeat Paxton, but he quickly walked back the comment, stating he would remain in the race.[33] Congressman Wesley Hunt entered the race in late 2025, further scrambling the race and increasing the chance of a runoff.[34]

All three candidates competed for the endorsement of Donald Trump, having made support for him and his agenda central to their campaigns; however, Trump declined to back a single candidate, instead stating he supported "all three".[35][36] Cornyn had maintained a substantial fundraising lead over the other candidates throughout the race, spending much of it attacking Paxton.[37] The early three-way polling was very narrow, usually with Cornyn and Paxton making the runoff and no candidate close to winning outright.[38] While campaigning, all three tapped into Islamophobic sentiment in their advertisements and actions, with Cornyn and Paxton having targeted the EPIC City development in Collin County with investigations and lawsuits.[39][40][41]

Cornyn led Paxton narrowly in the primary election, garnering 42.0% of the vote to Paxton's 40.5%, while Hunt placed a distant third with 13.5% of the vote.[152][153] Support for Cornyn and Paxton was relatively evenly spread across the state, though Cornyn performed slightly better in urban areas, especially Dallas and Austin, while Paxton performed slightly better in rural areas, particularly in East Texas.[154] Hunt performed slightly better in regions which backed Paxton, suggesting his presence on the ballot hurt Cornyn more than Paxton. Even in Hunt's own congressional district, he came in third with barely over 20% of the vote.[155]

In the days leading up to the March 3 primary, Paxton suggested he could win outright and avoid a runoff. However, Cornyn overperformed expectations in what The Texas Tribune described as a "better-than-expected showing". Rolando Garcia, a member of the State Republican Executive Committee who supported Hunt in the primary but planned to back Paxton in the runoff, said the result should alarm the Paxton campaign.[156] On March 5, The Atlantic reported that Trump advisers expected the president to endorse Cornyn in the runoff election after his unexpectedly strong performance in the first round of voting.[157]

Runoff

[edit]

Campaign

[edit]

Political observers described the runoff campaign between Paxton and Cornyn as "vile" and "brutal", featuring almost exclusively negative advertising from both sides.[158][159] Cornyn repeatedly attacked Paxton's character, especially regarding alleged infidelity towards his wife, state senator Angela Paxton, who had filed for divorce on "biblical grounds", and compared his ethics to that of a "strip club owner."[160][161] He also highlighted the political scandals that have plagued Paxton's career, including his 2023 impeachment by the Texas House of Representatives, framing him as corrupt and unfit for political office.[162] Paxton continued to frame Cornyn as insufficiently loyal to Donald Trump.[161][163] His office also drew scrutiny over a sharp increase in publicly-announced lawsuits made in his capacity as attorney general since announcing his Senate run and especially in the months immediately before the March primary. A sizeable number of these actions focused on issues salient to conservative voters, including immigration, Islam, DEI, student protests, and elections, drawing accusations that he used his office to energize his voter base and boost his campaign ahead of the runoff.[164]

The runoff significantly fractured both the Republican electorate and officeholders in the state, many of whom worried that the money spent and political attacks exchanged during the contest could benefit Democratic nominee James Talarico. Talarico won his primary outright, avoiding a runoff and allowing him to shift his focus to the general election early.[159][165] Lieutenant governor Dan Patrick even warned that a depressed Republican turnout could jeopardize Republican control of the Texas House, though most others dismissed that as extremely unlikely, with many Republicans still expressing confidence that both Paxton and Cornyn could win the general election.[166][167][168]

Despite speculation following his first-place primary finish that Trump would endorse Cornyn, Trump did not endorse either candidate by the March 17 withdrawal deadline. Republicans had hoped the non-endorsed candidate would exit to avoid a costly runoff and allow the nominee to focus on the general election. However, Paxton refused to withdraw unless the Senate eliminated the filibuster to pass the SAVE America Act. Meanwhile, Cornyn, previously a staunch defender of the filibuster, signaled openness to reforming or bypassing it, as Trump indicated his endorsement could hinge on the bill's passage.[169][170] Both candidates continued to court Trump's endorsement to consolidate support from the party, but Trump remained neutral in the race over two months after initially signaling his intention to endorse one of them.[171] This jockeying included policy-related moves as well as superficial ones, such as a bill introduced by Cornyn to designate U.S. Route 287 as Interstate 47 to honor Trump.[172]

On May 19, one week before the runoff, Trump announced his endorsement of Ken Paxton.[173] U.S. representative Wesley Hunt, who finished third in the first round of the primary, also endorsed Paxton that day.[27]

Following the runoff, Cornyn indicated tacit support for Paxton, saying he would vote for him and would back the Republican ticket but would not actively campaign for him.[174]

Paxton defeated Cornyn with 64% of the runoff vote, becoming the first challenger to defeat an incumbent senator in a primary election in the state since Lloyd Bentsen defeated Ralph Yarborough in 1970.[226] Cornyn became the second senator in the 2026 election cycle to lose renomination, after Bill Cassidy in Louisiana. His loss largely mirrored Cassidy's, performing best in the state's most Democratic-leaning areas, as well as wealthier suburban areas. Excluding sparsely populated Kenedy County, Cornyn only won Travis County, home to the state capital Austin, a heavily left-leaning area, while narrowly losing Dallas County, home to the wealthy Park Cities and Southern Methodist University.[227] Paxton's runoff performance was the largest for a second-place finisher in a U.S. Senate primary in Texas, eclipsing Charles A. Culberson's previous record in 1916.[228]

Democratic primary

[edit]

Background

[edit]

Democrats, who have not won a statewide election in Texas since 1994, see an opening in the state due to the bitter and divisive primary fight in the Republican side, a potential midterm backlash against the Trump administration, negative approval ratings for President Trump in Texas, as well as recent polling numbers showing competitive matchups.[229][230][231][232]

Colin Allred, who unsuccessfully ran against incumbent Republican senator Ted Cruz in 2024, exited the race on December 8, 2025, which precipitated Jasmine Crockett's entry into the race.[233]

Campaign

[edit]

Crockett entered the race with high name recognition and strong polling numbers, but her launch on the last day to file meant she had limited time for campaigning statewide.[234] According to polling data in February 2026 prior to the primaries, Crockett originally had a favorability percentage of 23%, and an unfavorable percentage of 25% while Talarico came in at 18% favorable and 9% unfavorable.[235][236] She did not hire a campaign manager, and focused on advertising over a staffed field operation.[237]

Crockett and Talarico participated in a debate on January 24, 2026, hosted by the AFL-CIO in Georgetown. During the debate, both candidates largely aligned on policy and engaged in limited direct attacks. Crockett defended her "firebrand" style as necessary for the political moment, while Talarico emphasized a more measured approach and his perceived electability against Ken Paxton.[238] Talarico later faced controversy after a social media influencer alleged he had referred to former rival Colin Allred as a "mediocre Black man" in comparison to Crockett in a private conversation; Talarico disputed the claim as a mischaracterization. Allred subsequently endorsed Crockett and criticized Talarico.[239] The episode further exposed the racial tension between each candidate's base of support, with Crockett performing best among Black voters, Democrats' strongest voter base, and Talarico performing best among White and Latino voters, demographics which hold far more swing voters.[240]

On February 16, Talarico was scheduled to appear on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert. According to Colbert, however, CBS did not allow him to air the interview nor mention the cancellation on-air based on a recently revised interpretation of the FCC's equal-time rule, although he did discuss it during that night's episode in spite of FCC threats. Colbert later posted the interview to the show's YouTube page.[241] The interview gained millions of views online, while Talarico fundraised $2.5 million in the aftermath and increased his name recognition as early voting began ahead of the March 3 primary. Analysts largely viewed the campaign as one based on personality and electability rather than ideology.[242]

After the primary, Crockett conceded to Talarico,[243] announcing support for his candidacy, but she declined to actively campaign for him.[244]

James Talarico won the Democratic primary with 52.4% of the vote.[310] After a dispute concerning voting hours in Dallas and Williamson Counties on the night of the primary, Crockett conceded the race on March 4.[311] The dispute in Dallas County arose from the county Republican Party's decision not to use countywide voting centers, where voters can cast ballots at any location, on Election Day, as Texas law requires both parties to agree in order to implement them.[312] On March 17, the Dallas County GOP announced it would use countywide voting centers for the runoff.[313]

Issues with a ballot scanning and tabulation machine in Newton County led to the county clerk writing in a court filing that its Democratic statewide primary results, with Hassan winning the county, were "skewed" and that a recount was required, which eventually had to be done by hand due to the scanning issues persisting,[314][315] with the revised results showing Crockett winning the county.

Democrats cast more primary votes in a midterm election than Republicans for the first time since 2002.[155] The results largely mirrored those of the 2020 primary for this seat, which also pitted a Black Democrat from Dallas (Royce West) against a White Democrat from the Austin area (M. J. Hegar). Crockett performed best among Black voters, winning by large margins in East Texas, as well as by smaller margins in the urban centers of Dallas and Harris counties. Talarico won the White and Hispanic vote, dominating in the Austin metro area, and winning the state's remaining rural areas, including the heavily-Hispanic Rio Grande Valley.[154]

Libertarian convention

[edit]

The Libertarian Party convention was held from April 10 to 12, 2026, in Abilene.[316] Ted Brown, the party's U.S. senate nominee in 2024, secured the nomination with 83 votes to Daniel "Mark" Sims's 39.[317]

General election

[edit]

Campaign

[edit]

Following the May Republican runoff, both nominees quickly pivoted to the general election.[318] Paxton's victory was welcomed by Democrats who viewed him as a weaker opponent, leading several nonpartisan forecasters to rate the race as more competitive.[226] Talarico adopted a more aggressive strategy, highlighting allegations that led to Paxton's impeachment by fellow Republicans.[319]

Economy

[edit]

Both Talarico and Paxton launched campaigns related to economic issues: Talarico's economic plan is named the "New American Dream," while Paxton's is named "Protecting the Texas Promise".[320] Talarico supports raising the minimum wage, canceling medical debt, and passing universal childcare and paid family leave.[320] Paxton supports tax deductions for healthcare, housing, and family-related expenses.[320]

Social and legal issues

[edit]

Paxton portrayed Talarico as an extremist, emphasizing culture war issues and gender, while criticizing his statement that "God is non-binary" and questioning his masculinity.[321][322] Paxton also repeatedly called Talarico a vegan, claiming "you can't get elected as a vegan in Texas," prompting Talarico to release photos and videos of himself eating meat and other non-vegan foods at campaign events.[323] In June, Talarico criticized the Attorney General's office over its handling of a child sexual abuse case involving former attorney Adam Hoffman during Paxton's tenure.[324] After a mistrial, Hoffman received a plea deal critics called "unusually lenient" and an "Epstein-style sweetheart deal," as it did not require him to register as a sex offender.[325] Talarico and John Cornyn had previously aired campaign ads criticizing Paxton over the case.[326][327]

Party unification

[edit]

Both Talarico and Paxton have faced challenges unifying their parties after the primaries, with limited support from former rivals exposing weaknesses in their coalitions.[328] Talarico has sought to bolster support among Black voters after defeating Jasmine Crockett, who skipped the state Democratic convention and declined to commit to campaigning for him, raising concerns about Black turnout.[329] Paxton has struggled with moderate Republicans who backed John Cornyn, with polls showing some Cornyn voters supporting Talarico.[328] Cornyn has also declined to fundraise for Paxton, instead focusing on competitive Senate races in other states.[330]

In part to rally support behind candidates such as Paxton, the Republican Party hosted its first-ever midterm national convention in Dallas on September 9 and 10.[331] After the midterm convention, Paxton said in a private conversation that the convention had a negative effect for the Republican Party.[332]

Attempts of holding debate

[edit]

On July 16, the Paxton and Talarico campaigns announced negotiations for up to three general election debates.[333] If held, they would mark Paxton's first debates since becoming a statewide elected official.[334][335][336] By September, Talarico had accepted a fourth invitation to a debate as Paxton had remained noncommittal, but insisted that they were still negotiating and expected to participate in at least one debate before the election.[337] Responding to a challenge issued by Talarico to appear on the channel,[338] a fifth debate invitation was issued by Fox News.[339] In early October, president Donald Trump and several other prominent Republicans called on Paxton to debate Talarico.[340] As of October 18, 2026[update], Paxton has not accepted an invitation to a single debate with Talarico.[341]

Election administration

[edit]

The election is taking place amidst a broader push by the Trump administration to restrict mail-in voting, although these efforts are currently mired in court proceedings.[342] On September 1, commissioners in Tarrant County, Texas's third-largest county, voted to close roughly a third of its polling locations, a year after cutting early-voting sites in half, citing cost savings at low-turnout locations. Critics warned the closures could increase travel times and suppress turnout.[343] Later that month, Votebeat reported that the Department of Public Safety had failed to distribute nearly 200,000 voter registrations to counties over the course of the past year due to a technical error, sparking a bipartisan outcry.[344] By the beginning of October, the reported size of the backlog had neared 600,000 registrations.[345] The backlog was sent to counties all at once, with many of the state's urban counties receiving tens of thousands one month before early voting was set to begin.[344] The state agreed to reimburse counties for the overtime pay incurred processing the glut of applications.[346] Observers and election experts highlighted the debacle as an example of the difficulties involved in registering to vote in Texas, one of the only states in the country to not offer universal online voter registration.[347]

Fundraising

[edit]

Talarico has considerably outraised Paxton throughout the campaign. Due to the high national profile of the race, both candidates, especially Talarico have received significant contributions from voters across the country. Within Texas, Talarico's donation base is concentrated in his home city of Austin and the state's other urban areas, while Paxton's is in Dallas.[447] Despite Talarico's individual fundraising advantage, however, leading into the fall campaign season, and particularly after the Republican National Convention in Dallas, Paxton has seen a massive infusion of political action committee and political party spending on his behalf to try to buoy his sagging polling numbers.[448] The Senate Leadership Fund alone committed over $100 million to support Paxton, far exceeding Talarico's individual fundraising numbers, though a remarkably high investment to defend a seat in a state Republicans have not lost in over 30 years.[449] Elon Musk also donated $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group supporting Ken Paxton.[450] The Supreme Court over the summer additionally cleared the way for political parties themselves to freely coordinate advertising spending with candidates at the candidates' reduced rate, handing Republicans a monetary advantage across the country due to the Democratic Party lagging behind the Republicans in party fundraising.[451] The Talarico campaign raised $64 million in the third quarter of 2026, the largest quarterly total by a U.S. Senate candidate ever, surpassing the $57 million record that had been set by Jaime Harrison in the 2020 South Carolina senate race.[452][453]
